title: Shloka 11
subtitle: The lute silenced, and a mind gone under

namas.translation: The sweetness of her ordinary conversation silences the kacchapī lute, which had until then been the standard of sweet sound.

compound.gloss: she by whom the kacchapī lute is put to shame through the sweetness of her speech

children.gloss: rebuked by the sweetness of her own speech
the sweetness of her own conversation
a lute so named for its tortoise-shaped body

namas.gloss: In Whose Smile Kāmeśa's Mind Is Drowned
namas.translation: Light spills from her faint smile in such quantity that the mind of her consort sinks and is lost in it.

compound.gloss: she in the flood of whose gentle smile the mind of Kāmeśa lies submerged

children.gloss: sinking in the flood of light from a soft smile
the flood of radiance of her gentle smile
the mind of the lord of desire
lord of desire, Śiva as her consort
the mind, that which belongs to the mind

commentary.meaning: Still the mouth, but no longer its parts — now what comes out of it. The first name sets her speech against the kacchapī, the lute that belongs to the goddess of speech herself, and the lute loses; and the word chosen for what she says is not song, not mantra, not oratory, but sallāpa, ordinary friendly talk. Her chat outsings the best instrument there is. The second name goes back to the smile the hymn has been circling since the tenth verse and finds a new thing for it to do: light comes off it in such quantity that the mind of her husband sinks and does not come up. Both names describe an effect on somebody else rather than a feature of her, which is a change of method. The description pauses to record two casualties — an instrument shamed into silence, and a mind under water — and the second casualty is the first appearance in this hymn of the god she is married to.
commentary.history:
Kacchapī is a female tortoise. Monier-Williams gives that sense first and then adds the second: a kind of lute, so named because it is shaped like a tortoise, and he cross-refers to the Latin testudo — the shell-bodied instrument of the classical Mediterranean, the Greek chelys, which was made from a real tortoise. The dictionary is pointing at a coincidence between two unrelated musical traditions, and it happens to be exactly right about why the Sanskrit word exists: the resonator is a curved bowl. In the Indian tradition Kacchapī is the proper name of Sarasvatī's instrument, as Mahatī is the name of Nārada's. So the first name of this verse is not comparing her speech to a lute in general. It is naming a specific instrument belonging to a specific goddess and saying that this goddess's small talk defeats it.

Śaṅkara stages the whole scene, and reading his verse beside the name is the quickest way to see what the sixteen syllables are compressing. Sarasvatī is singing Śiva's exploits to her lute. Devī begins to say something appreciative and moves her head as she says it. That is all: one word of praise, offered in passing. And the sweetness of it so contradicts the delicate ringing of the strings that Vāṇī, without a word, slips the cloth cover back over her vīṇā and puts it away. Nothing is announced and nobody is humiliated in public. The Vāgdevatās fold that into a single participle.

That participle is worth pressing on. Vinirbhartsita is built on the causative of a root that means to threaten, to scold, to revile — Monier-Williams glosses the related noun bhartsana as threatening, menace, curse — and it is armed with two prefixes, vi and nis, which push it to an extreme. So the lute has not merely been surpassed. It has been shouted down. The two names of the ninth verse defeated coral and the bimba fruit, but those were fruit and stone; this is the first time the losing party in one of these contests is a person, and the verb has become correspondingly harsh. There is a small joke in that harshness, since what does the shouting down is the gentlest sound in the poem.

The second half returns to a construction the hymn used twenty-two names ago and repeats it almost exactly. The sixth name was nijāruṇaprabhāpūramajjadbrahmāṇḍamaṇḍalā: her own light, prabhā, in flood, pūra, with the world-eggs majjat, drowning in it. Here it is mandasmitaprabhāpūramajjatkāmeśamānasā: the light of her faint smile, in flood, with Kāmeśa's mind drowning in it. Same noun, same noun, same present participle, in the same order and the same metrical position. This is self-quotation across a distance, and the substitution at the end is the whole point. What went under the first time was the entire ring of world-eggs. What goes under this time is one mind. The scale shrinks and the claim grows, because of whose mind it is.

Kāmeśa, lord of desire, is Śiva under the name this tradition prefers for him, and nāma 28 is the first place in the whole text — meditation verses included — where the consort is named at all. He arrives already submerged. That is not accidental placement. The first verse of the Saundaryalaharī states the doctrine flatly: joined with Śakti, Śiva can act; without her he cannot stir. The stotra makes the same point without arguing it, by choosing the moment of his first appearance to describe him as unconscious in her light.

One small thing the vocabulary allows, which may or may not have been meant. Mānasa is an ordinary word for the mind, and Monier-Williams also records it as the name of the lake Mānasa in the Himālaya, the water the wild geese are supposed to fly to. Kāmeśamānasa can be heard, without any violence to the grammar, as Kāmeśa's lake — which is a convenient thing to be drowning in. The hymn does not say this. The language makes it available.
commentary.practice:
Two sixteen-syllable names, one to a line, and for once both caesurae fall in a helpful place. Count eight in the first line and you land exactly at the end of mādhurya: nijasallāpamādhurya, then vinirbhartsitakacchapī. Count eight in the second and you land at the end of pūra: mandasmitaprabhāpūra, then majjatkāmeśamānasā. In both cases the break in the metre is also a break in the compound, so the natural breath and the natural sense agree. That is not always true in this hymn and it is worth enjoying when it happens.

Sallāpa hides a rule. The underlying form is saṃlāpa, from sam plus √lap, to talk; the nasal has assimilated forward into the l and doubled it. Monier-Williams is severe about it and files sallāpa as a wrong reading for saṃlāpa, but the doubled form is thoroughly current and it is what the stotra has. Say sal-lā-pa with the l held long enough to be counted twice, because the metre counts the first syllable heavy on the strength of it.

Vinirbhartsita is the hardest word in the verse and probably in the last five. Break it vi-nir-bhart-si-ta. The r of nir survives before a voiced consonant instead of becoming a visarga, so you get r running directly into the aspirated bh: let the breath be heard. Then bhart-si gives you r, an unaspirated dental t and a dental s in immediate succession, which is a sequence English never asks for. Slow it to three separate gestures and then close the gap. Note in passing that the nāmāvalī printed with this recension writes the dative as vinirbhatsitakacchapyai, without the r; the stotra line has it, and it belongs there.

Kacchapī gives you the cch you met at radanacchadā in the ninth verse, but this time it is inside the stem rather than at a junction between words. Give the first c a clean closure before the aspirated ch, and keep both of them as affricates made at the hard palate, never as the k sound English would supply.

The second line is easier but has two places to lose. Majjat is the doubled palatal you have now met three times — ujjvalā at the end of verse two, majjat in verse three, ujjvalā again at the end of verse ten — and it must be heard as two j sounds. Immediately after it comes a t running into a k in majjatkāmeśa: both unvoiced, both stops, and the temptation is to swallow the t. Release it.

Vowel lengths carry the sense here. Nija is two short syllables and means one's own, innate; if you lengthen it, it becomes nothing. Mādhurya and kacchapī both end long. In the second line, manda, smita and majjat are all short and quick, and then prabhā, pūra, kāmeśa and mānasā open out into long vowels one after another — which is a fair imitation of a flood.

For the recitation as archanā, the two names take the dative in -yai: nijasallāpamādhuryavinirbhartsitakacchapyai namaḥ, mandasmitaprabhāpūramajjatkāmeśamānasāyai namaḥ. Notice that the ī-stem contracts to -yai while the ā-stem keeps a syllable and gives -āyai. Saying the two one after the other is the cleanest short lesson in feminine datives the hymn offers.

As for what to hold: this is the verse in which the poem stops looking and starts listening. The instruction it implies is unusually concrete. Attend to the fact that what defeated the best music available was not a performance but a passing remark, and that what put the god of desire out of his mind was not a display but a slight smile. Nothing in this verse is done on purpose.

crossReferences.translation: Vāṇī is singing to her lute the many deeds of Paśupati; you begin to say a word of praise for it, with a movement of your head — and the sweetness of that word so gives the lie to the fine ringing of her strings that she quietly wraps her own vīṇā up in its cloth cover.
crossReferences.relevance: The scene the first name compresses, played out in full. Śaṅkara supplies the detail that makes the name intelligible: it is not a song of hers that beats the lute but a single remark made in passing, and the lute's owner takes the point herself and puts the instrument away without being told to. Note also the shared word mādhurya, sweetness, doing the same work in both texts.

crossReferences.translation: Mother, that tongue of yours is supreme: never resting from its telling over of the whole roll of your husband's virtues, and the colour of the hibiscus flower besides. Sarasvatī, who sits in front of it and whose form is a clarity like polished crystal, is turned by it into a body of ruby.
crossReferences.relevance: The other half of the same relationship. Here it is not Sarasvatī's instrument that gives way but Sarasvatī herself, who is transparent and therefore takes the red of the tongue in front of her. The verse also turns on the pun between japā, the hibiscus, and japa, muttered repetition — the same pun the fourth meditation verse of this stotra plays with, and a reminder that the tongue being praised is a tongue engaged in recitation.

crossReferences.translation: She in the flood of whose own dawn-red light the whole circle of world-eggs lies drowning.
crossReferences.relevance: The hymn quoting itself at twenty-two names' distance. Prabhā, then pūra, then majjat, in the same order and the same place in the line, and then a different thing being drowned. Setting the two names side by side shows the Vāgdevatās deliberately narrowing the aperture from the universe to a single mind, and expecting the reader to notice which of the two they think is the larger claim.

The tortoise comes first, the lute second, and the note comparing it to the Latin testudo is Monier-Williams's own — a rare moment where the dictionary lets you see an instrument being named for its shell in two unrelated traditions at once.

references.note: Verses 64 to 66 form a small group on her tongue, her mouthful of betel and her speech, and they run in the same order as the sahasranāma's tenth and eleventh verses. Read the three together and the parallel between the two texts becomes hard to dismiss as coincidence.
